title: HTTP: The Browser's Language
summary: Requests, responses, methods, and status codes behind every web page.

pages.title: Requests and responses
pages.body:
Every time you open a page, the browser sends an HTTP request to the server, and the server replies with a response.

A request contains:
- Method: what to do (GET, POST, etc.)
- Path: the page requested, e.g. /login
- Headers: extra info (browser type, cookies, language)
- Body: data being sent, e.g. form contents

A response contains a status code, headers, and the content (HTML, images, JSON).
pages.tip: A request is the order slip at a restaurant; the response is the food that arrives with the receipt.

pages.title: Common methods
pages.body:
- GET: fetch data. Parameters appear in the URL, e.g. /search?q=cats
- POST: send data, e.g. a login form. The data goes in the body
- PUT / PATCH: update data
- DELETE: remove data

Since GET parameters show in the URL, secrets like passwords must never be sent via GET. URLs end up in browser history, server logs, and shared links.
pages.tip: GET is a postcard: anyone holding it can read it. POST is a letter in an envelope.

pages.title: Status codes
pages.body:
A 3-digit number in the response that tells you the outcome:
- 2xx success, e.g. 200 OK
- 3xx redirect, e.g. 301 moved permanently
- 4xx client-side error: 401 not logged in, 403 forbidden, 404 not found
- 5xx server-side error, e.g. 500 Internal Server Error

For security analysts, status code patterns in logs are clues. Hundreds of 401s from one IP in a minute may mean someone is guessing passwords.
pages.tip: Status codes are like machine indicator lights: green is fine, yellow needs attention, red means trouble.

quiz.prompt: Which HTTP method should send a login form?
quiz.explanation: POST puts data in the body, not in a URL that ends up in history and logs.

quiz.prompt: Status 404 means...
quiz.explanation: 404 Not Found: the requested resource doesn't exist.

quiz.prompt: Status codes in the 5xx range indicate...
quiz.explanation: 5xx means the server failed to handle a valid request.

quiz.prompt: Hundreds of 401 responses to one IP in a minute likely signal...
quiz.explanation: 401 means failed authentication. Many at once suggests brute force.

quiz.prompt: The part of a request that carries cookies and browser info is the...
quiz.explanation: Headers carry request metadata, including cookies and the User-Agent.

title: Cookies & Sessions
summary: How sites remember you're logged in, and why session cookies are targeted.

pages.title: HTTP is forgetful
pages.body:
HTTP doesn't remember previous requests. Each request stands alone. So how does a site know you're logged in?

The answer: sessions. After a successful login, the server creates a random session ID and stores "this ID = Nadia". That ID is sent to the browser as a cookie, and the browser automatically sends it back with every later request.
pages.tip: A session cookie is a concert wristband. Checked once at the door; after that you just show the band.

pages.title: Session hijacking
pages.body:
Since a session cookie proves you're logged in, anyone who gets it can enter as you without your password, even bypassing 2FA.

How cookies get stolen:
- Malware or malicious browser extensions that siphon cookies
- XSS that reads cookies through JavaScript
- Logging in on a public computer and forgetting to log out

That's why "open this file" scams often turn out to be cookie stealers used to hijack YouTube, Instagram, and Facebook accounts.
pages.tip: If someone takes your wristband and wears it, the guard still lets them in.

pages.title: Secure cookie attributes
pages.body:
Developers can protect session cookies with attributes:
- HttpOnly: JavaScript can't read the cookie, so XSS has a hard time stealing it
- Secure: the cookie is only sent over HTTPS
- SameSite: the cookie isn't sent from other sites (helps prevent CSRF)
- Short lifetimes, and a fresh session ID after login

For users: log out on other people's devices, check "logged-in devices" on important accounts, and don't install random extensions.
pages.tip: Cookie attributes are like a wristband that can't come off without scissors and only works in this venue.

quiz.prompt: Why do sites need session cookies?
options: Because HTTP doesn't remember previous requests
quiz.explanation: Session cookies tie separate requests to one logged-in user.

quiz.prompt: An attacker gets your session cookie. What can they do?
quiz.explanation: A session cookie is proof of login. It can even bypass 2FA.

quiz.prompt: The HttpOnly attribute makes a cookie...
quiz.explanation: This reduces the risk of cookie theft via XSS.

quiz.prompt: The Secure attribute means a cookie is...
quiz.explanation: A Secure cookie is never sent over plain, unencrypted HTTP.

quiz.prompt: After logging in on an internet cafe computer, the most important step?
quiz.explanation: Closing a tab doesn't end the session. Logging out invalidates the session cookie.

title: XSS: Sneaky Scripts
summary: When user input turns into code running in other people's browsers.

pages.title: What XSS is
pages.body:
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) happens when a site displays user input as-is, without processing it. If that input contains a <script> tag, other visitors' browsers run it as code.

Example: a comment box shows raw text. An attacker posts a comment containing a script. Everyone who opens the page runs that script in their browser.
pages.tip: Picture a notice board that reads every note aloud over a loudspeaker, including one that says "everyone hand your wallet to me".

pages.title: Types and impact
pages.body:
Three main types:
- Stored: the script is saved in the database (comments, profiles) and hits every visitor
- Reflected: the script is in a link and hits whoever clicks it
- DOM-based: the page's own JavaScript mishandles input

The impact: stealing session cookies, swapping page content for a fake login form, or performing actions as the victim.
pages.tip: Stored is a trap set in the floor. Reflected is a trap wrapped as a gift and sent out.

pages.title: How to prevent it
pages.body:
The principle: user data must stay data, never become code.
- Output encoding/escaping: turn < into < before display, so it shows as text
- Use modern frameworks (Flutter, React, Vue) that escape automatically
- Input validation: reject things that clearly don't fit the format
- Content Security Policy (CSP): restrict where scripts may load from
- HttpOnly cookies as an extra layer

For users: be careful clicking long, strange links, even on real domains.
pages.tip: Escaping is like framing a note behind glass: still readable, but it can't be "spoken" as a command.

quiz.prompt: XSS happens because...
options: User input is displayed unprocessed and becomes code
The server runs out of memory
quiz.explanation: The core of XSS: user data runs as script in the browser.

quiz.prompt: XSS saved in a comment box that hits every visitor is called...
quiz.explanation: Stored XSS sits in the database and appears for every visitor.

quiz.prompt: The main defense against XSS is...
quiz.explanation: Escaping makes input display as text instead of running.

quiz.prompt: One impact of XSS is...
quiz.explanation: A script running in the victim's browser can read cookies (if not HttpOnly).

quiz.prompt: Content Security Policy (CSP) helps by...
options: Restricting which script sources may run
quiz.explanation: CSP tells the browser which script sources are allowed.

title: SQL Injection
summary: When form input rewrites the commands sent to the database.

pages.title: Databases and queries
pages.body:
Almost every app stores data in a database and retrieves it with SQL. An example login query:

SELECT * FROM users WHERE user = 'nadia' AND pass = '...'

The trouble starts when an app builds the query by gluing user input text directly into the command.
pages.tip: A query is like an order form the waiter fills in. It's dangerous if guests can write on the order slip directly.

pages.title: How injection happens
pages.body:
If input is glued in raw, a quote mark from the user can "close" the text early and the rest is read as a command. The classic example: ' OR '1'='1 makes the condition always true, so login succeeds without the right password.

SQL injection can be severe:
- Logging in without a password
- Reading all user data
- Modifying or deleting data

Many major data breaches began with this flaw.
pages.tip: Like a guest writing on the order slip: "1 fried rice, and give me the cash drawer." If the cook just obeys, trouble.

pages.title: The fix: parameterized queries
pages.body:
The fix is simple and powerful: never glue input into a query. Use parameterized queries (prepared statements):

SELECT * FROM users WHERE user = ? AND pass = ?

The database receives the command and the data separately, so any input is treated as data.

Extras:
- Use an ORM or query builder
- Give the database account minimal privileges
- Store passwords as hashes, not plain text

Practice attacks only in official labs like DVWA or TryHackMe, never on other people's sites.
pages.tip: A parameterized query is a form with locked fields: guests can only write in the "menu" box, not add new commands.

quiz.prompt: SQL injection happens when...
options: User input is glued directly into a database query
quiz.explanation: User text gets read as part of the SQL command.

quiz.prompt: Why can ' OR '1'='1 bypass login on a vulnerable app?
options: It makes the condition always true
quiz.explanation: The quote closes the text, then OR '1'='1' makes the WHERE clause always true.

quiz.prompt: The most effective defense against SQL injection is...
quiz.explanation: Command and data are sent separately, so input can't alter the command.

quiz.prompt: Where is the right place to practice SQL injection?
options: Official labs like DVWA or TryHackMe
quiz.explanation: Attacking systems without permission is illegal, including under Indonesia's ITE Law.

quiz.prompt: Why should an app's database account have minimal rights?
options: To limit damage if there's a flaw
quiz.explanation: Least privilege: if injection happens, the attacker can't do everything.

title: Access & the OWASP Top 10
summary: The most common web app flaws, starting with broken access control.

pages.title: Broken access control
pages.body:
Login proves who you are (authentication). Access control decides what you may do (authorization). The most common web flaws live right here.

IDOR example: your invoice page is /invoice?id=1042. If changing it to 1043 shows someone else's invoice, the server forgot to check "whose invoice is this".

The fix: the server must always check ownership and role on every request, and never trust anything the browser sends.
pages.tip: An office access card proves you're an employee, not that you may enter the director's room.

pages.title: The OWASP Top 10
pages.body:
OWASP is an open community that regularly publishes a list of the 10 most important web security risks. Some that always appear:
- Broken Access Control (like the IDOR above)
- Cryptographic Failures: sensitive data left unencrypted
- Injection: SQL injection, XSS, and friends
- Security Misconfiguration: default settings, error pages that leak info
- Vulnerable Components: outdated libraries with known flaws
- Authentication Failures: weak passwords allowed, no login attempt limits

The list is a reference for developers, auditors, and pentesters worldwide.
pages.tip: The OWASP Top 10 is like a list of "10 most common causes of fire": not everything, but checking these cuts the risk sharply.

pages.title: Safe developer habits
pages.body:
If you build your own apps, start here:
- Check authorization on the server for every endpoint
- Use parameterized queries and auto-escaping frameworks
- Update dependencies regularly (flutter pub outdated, npm audit)
- Never commit passwords or API keys to GitHub
- Turn off debug mode and detailed error messages in production
- Limit login attempts and support 2FA

Security isn't a feature bolted on at the end; it's a habit from the first line of code.
pages.tip: Fitting locks while building the house is cheaper than tearing down walls after a burglary.

quiz.prompt: The difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication = who you are, authorization = what you may do
Authentication = what you may do, authorization = who you are
quiz.explanation: Logging in (authentication) doesn't mean you may access everything (authorization).

quiz.prompt: Changing id=1042 to id=1043 in the URL shows someone else's data. This flaw is...
quiz.explanation: The server isn't checking who owns the requested data.

quiz.prompt: The OWASP Top 10 is...
options: A list of the best antivirus
A list of the most important web app security risks
quiz.explanation: Published by the OWASP community and used as a global reference.

quiz.prompt: Outdated libraries with known flaws fall under...
quiz.explanation: Vulnerable components make an app vulnerable even if its own code is clean.

quiz.prompt: Which developer habit is wrong?
quiz.explanation: Secrets in public repos can be found by bots within minutes.
